title: I am my beloved's (Song of Songs 6:3)
hookLine: "I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine"; tradition hears the month of Elul in its first letters

lines: ELUL, THE MONTH BEFORE ROSH HASHANAH.
cards: Four Hebrew letters: aleph, lamed, vav, lamed. Together they spell Elul, the month just before Rosh Hashanah. Tradition says that month is hiding inside one line of the Song of Songs.
Take the first letter of each of the line's first four Hebrew words, set them side by side, and there it is. A love song, carrying the name of a month on the calendar.

teach.b: I am my beloved's. The verse in full, in the JPS 1917 translation: "I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine, That feedeth among the lilies." In Hebrew: ani l'dodi v'dodi li.
Ani, I. L'dodi, to my beloved. V'dodi, and my beloved.
Li, to me. Aleph, lamed, vav, lamed: Elul. Earlier in the Song, nearly the same words come in the other order: "My beloved is mine, and I am his."
Some readers notice the turn. First she says he is hers. Later she begins with herself, given to him.
Love that starts with having becomes love that starts with giving. Why tie the line to Elul? Elul is the month of getting ready for the High Holy Days.
In Ashkenazi custom the shofar is sounded on weekday mornings through the month, until the day before Rosh Hashanah, and Psalm twenty-seven is added to the daily prayers.
It's a month for looking back, setting things right with people, and turning. The teaching about the letters, from later Jewish writers, says this turning needn't be a grim inspection.
It can be two who love each other walking back toward each other.

teach.h: FIRST HE IS MINE, THEN I AM HIS.
teach.b: Read that way, the people say the first half to God, I am my beloved's, and God's answer is folded into the same sentence: and my beloved is mine.

teach.h: ELUL: A MONTH OF TURNING BACK.
teach.b: The line has another life too.

teach.h: A COUPLE, AND A PEOPLE AND GOD.
teach.b: Some couples engrave it inside wedding rings or speak it under the wedding canopy. The same four words carry a marriage and a month of return.

how: The verse 'I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine' is taught as a hint to the name of Elul, the month before Rosh Hashanah, when Ashkenazi communities sound the shofar on weekday mornings and add Psalm 27 to the prayers.

games.why: the Elul teaching ties the month to 'I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine': turning back as love, going both ways.

practice: Let one person you love come to mind: a partner, a parent, a child, a friend who has stayed. Think of one way you are theirs, something you give, a way you show up, and one way they are yours.
If you pray, say the verse itself, slowly: ani l'dodi v'dodi li.
